newsitem.title: USA: U.S. concerned at China's supercomputer diversion.
newsitem.headline: U.S. concerned at China's supercomputer diversion.

text.p: The United States is concerned that China may have recently diverted American supercomputers from civilian to military use, the State Department said on Wednesday.

It said Secretary of State Madeleine Albright had raised the issue with China this week, but did not confirm details of a newspaper report that China had sent a U.S. supercomputer to a military research facility earlier this year.

The New York Times on Wednesday quoted U.S. officials as saying they determined two weeks ago that the computer did not reach its intended destination in Beijing. Instead, it was shipped to a defence and scientific research institute in Changsha, the Times reported.
"We are concerned that there have been recent diversions of supercomputers from civilian to military use in China," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
"We are looking into all of those. We're talking to the American companies involved, and we're talking to the Chinese government," Burns told a news briefing.

He said that at a meeting in Hong Kong this week with Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen, Albright had raised the issue "as one that had to be tracked very closely," but without getting into the details.
There were also sub-cabinet level discussions between U.S. and Chinese officials, he added.
"These are supercomputers with an MTOPS level which is quite low, which does not lead us to believe that the most advanced supercomputer technology has been diverted to military use," Burns said.
"But nonetheless, this is a very important issue. And we expect the Chinese government will look into this as closely as we are."
In mid-June, China dismissed U.S. charges that it had diverted purchase of U.S.-made supercomputers for military use. China contended they were used for scientific research.

The supercomputer was made by Sun Microsystems Inc and was sold to a Hong Kong company, which resold it to a scientific institute in Beijing, the Times said, quoting Under Secretary for Commerce for Export Administration William Reinsch.
A sale to a scientific institute would not require a license under the Clinton administration's 1995 policy on supercomputer exports.
However, Reinsch said the United States determined on June 19 that the supercomputer had been sent to a military and scientific research institute, which would require a license.
The U.S. Commerce Department was investigating the situation and the lack of a license, Reinsch said.
Reinsch said Chinese officials had been "somewhat helpful," but had turned down an American request to inspect the computer.

Unnamed U.S. officials were quoted as saying that China had told the United States that it did not intend to deceive anyone and that the supercomputer was always meant to go to Changsha, where it is to be used for peaceful purposes.
Burns said the Commerce Department was talking to American firms about improved methods whereby the firms could report on any signs that there might have been diversions.
